query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin hafnium (Hf) coating on a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a protective HfO₂ scale on the surface.
generation.material_initial_state: An uncoated refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a VZrHfNbTa-based alloy) intended for structural applications at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin Hf coating (approximately 120 μm thick) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Expose the coated and uncoated alloys in air at around 1000°C for an extended duration (e.g., 50 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, adherent HfO₂ layer at the coating/alloy interface that acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature oxidation, the Hf coating preferentially oxidizes to generate a stable and slow-growing HfO₂ layer. This oxide barrier reduces oxygen ingress into the underlying alloy matrix, thereby limiting further internal oxidation and preserving mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Hf-coated alloy will show significantly lower weight gain (indicative of reduced oxidation) and fewer signs of surface degradation compared to the untreated alloy under identical conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA exposed to the same high-temperature oxidizing environment exhibits higher mass gains and more pronounced oxidation-related degradation.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated to be most effective around 1000°C in a typical air atmosphere; performance under much lower or higher temperature regimes or different atmospheres (e.g., highly corrosive gases) remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance and the long-term stability of the HfO₂ scale beyond the test period are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples from the same batch of refractory HEA: one group with the Hf coating applied (~120 μm thick) and one group left uncoated. Expose both groups to an air atmosphere at 1000°C for 50 hours.
measurements: Determine the weight gain per unit area of both the coated and uncoated samples.
Perform surface and cross-sectional SEM imaging to assess oxide scale formation and morphology.
Conduct X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis to identify phase compositions and confirm the presence of HfO₂.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and improved surface/oxide scale quality compared to the uncoated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the continuous exploration of extreme environments such as deep space, deep sea, and outer space, there is an increasing requirement for functional materials capable of withstanding ultra-high and ultra-low temperatures. High-temperature alloys are the main materials serving as core components in frontier technologies such as aerospace and nuclear industries, such as engines, gas turbines, and high-temperature structural parts. These alloys require high strength, high-temperature fatigue resistance, oxidation resistance, and thermal corrosion capability. However, high-temperature and oxidation have become the primary problems that limit the further application of high-temperature alloys in extreme environments. Comprehensive consideration of existing high-temperature oxidation-resistant materials, the main high-temperature oxidation-resistant alloys used in engineering are iron, cobalt, and nickel-based alloys. The cost of iron-based high-temperature alloys is relatively lower, but poorer high-temperature stability. High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application.
